history:
Ladies was first played by Electron on 8/18/00, debuted on the same night as the full Chemical Warfare Brigade opera, along with Floodlights, Shelby Rose and Confrontation. The lyrics are largely the same, but the structure of the song is slightly different: there are shouts of “give it up! give it up!” in the introduction and before the jam, and there is a brief synth jam in between the verses. The jam in this Electron version is also considerably slower and mellower than in Biscuits versions, and there is no peak; rather, the jam just resolves back into the same verse from the intro.

The first and only Biscuits version of Ladies in 2000 is tightened up considerably from the Electron version. It is much faster than the Electron version, and the peak has that much needed Barber “oomph.” Although slightly slower than modern versions, in all other ways the song is virtually indistinguishable.

Ladies was played a whopping 27 times each in 2001 and 2002, the years of the song’s first golden age. It was a staple of the early spring tour, and was mostly played standalone, although it was split on its second performance on 3/22/01 and segued into on 4/12/01 and 4/20/01. It was inverted for the first time at the Bisco Knights festival on 8/25/01. In the fall tour the song became a powerhouse, with standout versions including the set closing standalone on 9/8/01 and the massive inverted version on 9/22/01.

2002 was the year Ladies really took off. 4/25/02 is the first dyslexic version, and the standout version from the spring tour. The summer tour included many excellent versions, including 7/26/02 and 8/11/02, but the real apex for the song came in the fall tour, with two legendary versions on 10/4/02 and 10/18/02.

Ladies became less common after 2002, and although the 2003 versions aren’t as legendary as the late 2001 or 2002 versions, there are a couple with unmistakable merit, such as the unfinished 4/25/03 or the split-up 11/28/03 (which was a part of the fourth complete performance of the Chemical Warfare Brigade. Ladies was only played seven more times with Sammy after 2003.

When Allen joined the band, Ladies became a catalog staple once again. Its second golden age lines up nicely with the second golden age of the band overall, beginning in mid-2007 and lasting into early 2010. The Astronaut > Ladies (><) > Astronaut from 11/19/06 is arguably the first great Ladies with Allen, but the spectacular 5/27/07 Ladies > O Fortuna > Spacebird (><) > Ladies and the over 35 minute Ladies > Gangster from 10/23/07 definitively assured Ladies’ place in the pantheon of trance-fusion juggernauts.

Ladies remained a powerhouse staple through 08 (standout versions including 1/16/08, 4/18/08, 5/24/08, 6/13/08 and 12/30/08), but the song hit another level in 2009, when it was played 21 times (the most of any year since 2002). In a year of furious lightspeed trance jams, Ladies flourished. Notable versions including 2/15/09, 4/24/09, and 6/25/09 are hailed as some of the best ever. The song was played twice in 2010 before wristgate, on 1/29/10 and 3/17/10, and both versions are excellent.

Ladies remained a setlist staple in the setbreak era, and in addition to the numerous versions played during this time, the band frequently used a Ladies style jam to get from A to B in this era. In fact, the year where Ladies was most common was 2012, when it was played on average once every 3.3 shows. Notable versions from the setbreak era include the 1/26/14 Tractorbeam version, 3/26/16, 6/02/16, and 8/20/16.

In the post-setbreak era, Ladies continues to be a setlist staple. It is still frequently played inverted, although well-known exceptions include the set bookending 9/23/23 and the dyslexic 1/28/24 (part of a full set palindrome). Ladies is one of the most frequently played Biscuits songs, appearing on average once every five to six shows since its debut. It has only disappeared from the rotation for more than a dozen shows a few times, and never for more than sixteen shows. It is an indisputably important part of the Biscuits’ catalog.

title: Akira Jam
history:
For the 2nd set on New Years Eve, 1999, The Disco Biscuits played along to Katsuhiro Otomo's anime masterpiece, Akira. Starting with just the setbreak DJ spinning, the band members slowly came out one by one onto stage dressed entirely in black robes. Behind them a on a projection screen, the movie played. This "Akira Jam" eventually falls into Basis For a Day to end the set.

As for syncing up the taped set to the movie itself, this is a topic under heavy debate among Biscuits fans. There are many theories as to where you should start the tape with the movie, so it might take you some experimenting to find the best sync. Although there is no real preferred method, the following tip can help you get the sync right:

"When the 1988 dateline appears, the first note of the DJ spinning should start up. When they first take off in the motorcycles, the beat should get noticeably more intense. When the kid is headbutted by the big Clown leader, the drum machines should stop completely, leaving just the vocal sample. When the first child subject screams after seeing his guardian shot, a phone should ring right at the time the store sign blows up (right before the windows all smash). Hope that will help line it up."

history:
Supposedly written after Barber told his convenience store boss to fuck off, Aceetobee was one of the earliest originals debuted by the Biscuits, alongside Barfly, Pat & Dex, and Basis. It features an intro, a verse section, a composed bridge, a vamp on the middle section with a descending riff, and a jam section built around a captivating, uplifting riff.

In the early trance-fusion era, the most interesting Aceetobee jams were intro jams segued into from other songs. One of the earliest Biscuits jams of note is 11/18/97 Vassillios > Aceetobee. These two were also paired together on 8/28/98 at the Wetlands to similarly great effect.

Aceetobee began to develop into a more full-fledged jam vehicle in 1999. 3/14/99 was the first Aceetobee to divert from the usual formula. Instead of a triumphant rock jam, the main jam was brooding and atmospheric until turning on a dime back into Aceetobee. 3/27/99 is another lauded version, mainly for the type two intro jam.

Spring 1999 saw some of the first significant developments in Aceetobee, notably the expansion of the hitherto underutilized “first jam” section. 4/10/99 (another contender for greatest) is the first version to be split in the first jam section, sandwiching the underutilized Smoothie King (and featuring another fantastic intro jam and soaring main jam). 4/24/99 is perhaps the first Aceetobee to feature a lengthy first jam, one that is, in fact, nearly as long as the second or “main” jam. After these developments, Aceetobee remained largely stagnant for the remainder of the year, but some standout versions include 9/20/99 and 9/28/99. Beyond these, Aceetobee was mainly of interest for the jams into the song rather than the jams in the song itself. For some excellent segues into Aceetobee, see 5/29/99, 9/15/99 and 10/9/99.

From 2000 to 2002, Aceetobee did not develop much. Despite this, there are plenty of standout versions from this era. Aceetobees in this era were consistent if fairly predictable, and fans of the song have a variety of solid versions to choose from. Some of these are 7/12/00 (played with Jordan Crisman on bass), 8/26/00, 11/10/00, 9/19/01 (a beautiful, spacey 27 minute version), 12/31/01, 8/13/02 (first inverted), 8/18/02 (actually goes type two in the main jam) and 10/5/02 (from the legendary Haymaker festival).

The second show of 03 featured a gorgeous, fleshed out Aceetobee, and it seems like every version played that year was an attempt to top the last. For this reason, just about every Aceetobee played in 03 is spectacular and worth hearing. The highlights are 4/4/03, 4/25/03, 9/29/03, and 11/29/03. Two additional highlights merit further discussion: 7/26/03, spectacular in its own right, is the second inverted version, and is inverted middle > end > beginning unlike the 02 version which is inverted end > beginning > middle. 10/23/03 is the first ever techno Aceetobee; it was played at a Perfume show, but the techno Aceetobee was played a few times at standard Biscuits shows.

In 2003, Aceetobee was played more frequently than any year since 1999. 2004-2005 Aceetobee was relegated to a more secondary role. 11/27/04 stands out as a stellar version for any era, and 8/27/05 sandwiches an inverted Nughuffer in a poignant moment in Sammy’s last show.

When Allen joined the band, Aceetobee became considerably rarer, and was played almost always as a standalone, and frequently as a set closer. It had a brief mini-renaissance beginning in July 2007. 7/8/07 features Aceetobee inside a Bazaar Escape sandwich (rare in itself), and 7/13/07 is an excellent version, with an Aceetobee > Pilin’ it Higher > Aceetobee sandwich stuck in the middle of a Crystal Ball palindrome. 10/16/07 features an excellent type two jam in the main section, and 11/4/07 Aceetobee > Great Abyss > Aceetobee is maybe the best version of the year.

After a strong 2007, Aceetobee was only played twice in 2008, 4/18/08 and 6/6/08. Both of these versions are very solid. It may have ran out of steam from being played so infrequently, as the 09 versions were generally not as strong as the ones from 07-08. 7/1/09 is probably the only standout version from this year, and there are many versions that are the weakest part of significant segments (4/23/09, 6/25/09, 10/4/09).

Aceetobee continued to play second fiddle to the major heavy hitters throughout the rest of 2.0 and the setbreak era. On 11/22/09, the song Catalyst developed out of an Aceetobee first jam. The Aceetobee > Catalyst > Aceetobee pairing further limited Aceetobee’s jam potential, and was played a total of five times besides the debut.

Besides the revisiting of the techno Aceetobee on 6/8/10, there were very few significant versions of the song between 2009 and 2017. In 2017 the song had another mini renaissance; it was played on average once every six shows, more frequently than any year since 2011. Each of these versions is worth hearing. 4/29/17 at the Capitol Theatre features a fantastic split Aceetobee with a drawn out intro jam segued from Papercut. Aceetobee was inverted for the third time ever on 5/28/17, and the middle was played at the Ogden on 6/1/17, completing this first and only split inversion of the song. The Aceetobee > Abyss > Aceetobee pairing was dusted off, to great success, on 9/21/17 at Irving Plaza, and Aceetobee was segued into from the Mario theme, and used to sandwich an excellent set of video game music, on 12/31/17 at the Playstation Theatre. Easily the best version of the year, and possibly the best version with Allen, was the techno Aceetobee played 11/17/17 at the Fillmore in Denver.

After this mini-renaissance, Aceetobee remained a once-or-twice-per-year rarity. The song rarely delivers show-defining highlights, but there are still occasional versions worth checking out: 9/16/23 is the strongest since 11/17/17, and 12/1/23 the first techno version since that date.

title: Anthem
history:
Part of the slew of debuts from the Setbreak is Over tour, Anthem soon became the clear favorite of the band. It was played eight times over the tour, more than any other song (for comparison, Electric Slinky and Station were the next most played at six times). Anthem is an instrumental in the vein of Orch Theme, with a simple composed riff repeated, with a short jam section in the middle. It was widely assumed that Anthem would be used as the New Years countdown song and that assumption was borne out.

Along with Running into the Night, Anthem was one of the most successful debuts from this era in the following years. It was played 12 times in 2021 and 11 times in 2022. After 5 performances in 2023 (all in the first half of the year) it was shelved indefinitely as the Revolution in Motion songs began to take up more of the setlist.

Anthem was typically used as little more than a high-energy peak in jams, but by the summer of 2022 it began to take on a character of its own. Of particular note is the "unfinished" 8/26/22 version, which sees the band transform into a dubby groove out of what had been a fairly rigid jam structure. Most of the versions after this one are worth checking out, but especially 10/30/22, 11/13/22, and 5/21/23.

history:
7-11, in its earliest stage, almost feels like a symbolic statement on the band. It debuted 3/11/00, the first show after Marc Brownstein was fired, a show rife with experimentation, new ideas and techniques. A morose breakup song with a resigned yet optimistic and somewhat fuck-it-all refrain seems very fitting for this mood.

Before the debut, Barber told the audience that the song came from “a very emotional time… I was working a 7-11, and then I got back to 7-11 and the song was in the rotation. We’re going to play it once. Only today.” Shortly before its second performance, Barber told the audience that people had been telling him to keep it in the rotation.

Perhaps no song changed as much from its debut as 7-11. The earliest versions of the song, called “Bring Your Ass to the Party” until its first rework in 2001, were considerably slower and the lyrics much less polished and rawer than later versions. There is a poignant personalness to the lyrics in the 2000 versions not present in the post-rework versions: take for example the line, “girl, I even wrote a rock opera for you, it wasn’t enough, it wasn’t enough.” The distinct “I’m gonna go out and jam” refrain is present and largely the same as modern versions, but the pre-chorus is absent and the verses are very different.

Bring Your Ass to the Party was played six times before being shelved, five without Marc Brownstein. The jam section, like the song itself, was considerably rawer than with modern iterations, often resulting in wild exploratory jams. The best example of this is the only version played with the full band before the song was reworked, 8/26/00 at Camp Bisco, sandwiched between the debut of Home Again. The segues into and out of Bring Your Ass to the Party put this segment in easy contention for the best versions ever played of both songs.

After Camp Bisco, Bring Your Ass to the Party was shelved until it was debuted again, reworked and rebranded as 7-11, on 6/27/01 at the private show at Lisa Klein’s house. This show also featured the debuts of The Tunnel and the Spy rework. The differences in the song structure are numerous and profound. The song was much faster post-rework, and the lyrics no longer make reference to a breakup. The composition is considerably more fleshed out as well. The “maybe all that you want to be is all that you have to be” pre-chorus/ending and the “towel” bridge were both added--and, in fact, prior to the rework, the song didn’t really have an ending at all.

7-11 became a staple of the fall tour of 2001, which is replete with standout versions of the song, most notably 9/9/01. The band also became more adventurous with the song structure. It was split up for the first time on 8/8/01, split up at the middle (or towel section) on 9/14/01 and 9/15/01, and inverted on 12/1/01.

7-11 remained a staple of the band’s catalog after the rework, not disappearing from the rotation for more than 40 shows, however it still was not fully finished. 3/9/02 is a particularly interesting version, featuring both the first verse referencing a breakup and the distinctive heavy intro riff; the former was not standard until 8/7/02 and the latter not until 9/28/02. Additionally, the Perfume version, often called Wawa, was introduced on 5/28/03. Despite the fact that it was played only the once, it has remained a popular request ever since.

The song remained solid for the remainder of Sammy’s tenure, particularly in the fall of 2002. 9/28/02 was the first three part version and 11/9/02 the second and final until 1/4/20. Other significant versions from this era include 10/19/02 and 10/26/02.

7-11 remained in the rotation after Allen joined the band, but over the years the ending became rarer and rarer. Allen played the ending for the first time on 10/19/07, whereupon it reentered the rotation sporadically. It was played two more times in 2007, twice in 2008, twice in 2009, then shelved again until 2014.

7-11 was especially strong in the golden years of 2.0, 2007 and 2009. 10/26/07 stands head and shoulders above the others from the year, although they’re all fairly consistent. 2009 was possibly the best year for the song; the most notable versions include 2/25/09, 6/4/09, 9/25/09, and 10/2/09. The song was only played three times in 2010, but all three are worthwhile.

The song remained in fairly steady rotation in the setbreak era with at least one or two per year. It became fairly interesting again in 2018, with two massive contenders for GOAT status: 5/24/18, a type two full version complete with outro, and 12/28/18, an unfinished version with two lengthy jams including one of the longest towel jams ever.

After setbreak was declared to be over, the song became somewhat more of a rarity, appearing only twice per year in 2020-2022 and just once in 2023. Of these versions, 4/8/22 is notable as being the fourth three-part 7-11 ever, and 10/16/21 is worth hearing for a particularly strong towel jam.

history:
“This song is called Basis for a Day, it’s a song you should listen to every day” - Barber, 10/1/98

Stunning and majestic, Basis for a Day is the likeliest candidate for consensus greatest song in the Disco Biscuits catalog. The catalog is replete with 30 and 40 minute versions, three part versions, and numerous versions that are considered among the best jams ever played. The song itself is rather simple: a modern standalone version usually consists of a drawn out intro jam, a composed middle (which features a triumphant two chord riff, a chorus of “whoa”s from the band, a bass slap section (sometimes jammed out, as in a three part version), a (relatively) complex instrumental section, a reprise of the triumphant “whoa” section, and an ending riff), an even more drawn out main jam, and a triumphant peak. After the peak, the band stops, and then plays a quick high-energy jam back into the same peak, after which the ending riff from the composed middle is repeated (this is sometimes known as the tag, or Gimme All Your Fucking Money (GAYFM) section, after a line Brownstein sometimes yells to the crowd).

Because 1995 and 1996 are not represented in the Biscuits archives, it is hard to know exactly how much Basis grew in those early years and how different the modern version is from the early version. Luckily, one Basis from before 1997 is still readily available in circulation: 8/7/96 at the band’s first show at the Wetlands Preserve, immortalized on the earliest edition of Encephalous Crime. This early version is vastly different from the modern version. The intro jam is less than two minutes long, and features a bizarre stream of consciousness narration from Barber. The iconic whoas are absent from the composition, as is the bass slap section, but otherwise the composed middle is fairly similar to modern versions. The main jam is under ten minutes and sees the narration from Barber continue. Rather than building to the distinctive peak, the main jam breaks down, at which point the band plays the ending riffs, and build up to a crescendo before dropping back into that riff.

Until May 2020, the earliest extant Basis on Archive was 1/30/97, but that changed with the release of 1/17/97 from the vaults. The Basis on this version has some notable differences from the EC Basis: the first whoas are sang, and the ending is different: rather than building straight to the ending riffs, the jam builds up to the distinctive Basis peak that we know today, after which there is a tag section which builds up to the ending riffs (the peak is not played a second time). At some point after 8/7/96, but no later than 1/17/97, this iconic peak riff was added. 1/30/97, the first three-part Basis and for years the earliest extant Archive Basis, saw further developments to the song structure, namely the addition of the distinctive bass slap section to the composed middle. This section developed organically out of an intro jam, led by Brownie, into the middle of Basis.

After 1/30/97, there are another eleven versions of Basis from 1997 available on Archive. 2/22/97 is the first version in which the band plays the peak a second time in the tag section, although this didn’t become standard right away (3/25 and 4/12 are not played this way, for example). 3/25/97 and 5/13/97 feature more of the bizarre stream of consciousness narration present on the EC version. 3/29/97 is a somewhat odd version in which the band almost inverts the song, playing the peak before dropping (somewhat clumsily) into an intro. After 5/31/97 there are no Bases on Archive until 11/17/97; despite this gap, the song doesn’t seem to have grown much, although the band is playing tighter. The band played a Basis ending on 12/27/97 and followed up the next two nights with full versions of Basis, illustrating how important the song had become to the catalog by then. 12/28/97 is the longer and stronger version, and features an interesting type two breakdown (shades of Aceetobee and perhaps Peter Gunn from Barber?) towards the end of the main jam that showcases Magner’s new electronic synth capabilities.

The first golden era for Basis began in 1998. Basis was played 34 times in 1998, and of this number 25 have survived into circulation on Archive. The first Basis of the year is short and unassuming, not at all portentous of the song’s future role as the band’s heaviest hitter of the year, but the second version is a massive two song pairing, an over 50 minute Run Like Hell > Basis for a Day combo that skyrocketed both of these songs into the stratosphere. Other important early 98 versions include 3/21/98 Law and Order Theme > Basis, the 4/2/98 medley (which features an impressive DJ segue out of the bass slaps to a Shem-Rah intro), 4/18/98 Vassillios > Basis (featuring, of all things, a didgeridoo, but more importantly the first Basis to feature a trance jam), and 5/2/98 Basis > Dribble > Run Like Hell > Basis (another important show for Run Like Hell, as well as Dribble). Basis turned another corner on 7/3/98, which featured a nearly 40 minute version of the song, by far the longest yet. This version is emblematic of all the developments in the song over the course of 1998: the intro jam is ten minutes long, thematic and interesting in a way the earlier versions were not. The main jam is over 23 minutes even if you don’t include the tag, a relentless breakneck 98 style trance jam that had become the norm for the song. It holds up to modern versions as one of the best Bases ever. Basis was particularly strong for the remainder of the year, with important versions including 8/15/98, 9/9/98, and 12/29/98 (the last of which was included on the reissue of Encephalous Crime).

“The song’s called Basis for a Day… and it changes over time as the band changes over time. And so we took a really hot version from a couple weeks ago, digitally mastered it, and put it on the end of the album, so the album’s a little more up-to-date than it used to be.” - Barber, 2/05/99

The meteoric rise of Basis continued into 1999. Two very solid versions, 1/21/99 and 1/26/99, preceded a monumental version, 1/29/99, which at the time was probably the best version ever played. The band followed this with a nearly 40 minute version on 2/5/99 that is a little bloated at times and overall not as strong as the 40 minute version from 7/3/98. After this version it was nothing but smooth sailing for Basis in winter 1999. The next version, 2/10/99 (also an important date for M.E.M.P.H.I.S.) featured the first jamming on the middle of Basis, or out of the bass slap section, a trend that continued sporadically throughout the year and beyond. 2/19/99, which opens with the powerful Pygmy > Basis ending combo, is the first dyslexic Basis and arguably the first dyslexic Biscuits song (there is a Harry Hood from 1996 that is notated as dyslexic). Other standouts from the rest of the tour include 2/25/99, 3/6/99, and 3/18/99. A short anecdote from 3/27/99 stands out as evidence that Basis had become the most important song in the catalog. The band had left the stage after the encore, but were determined to play the end of Basis one more time before tour ended. They got back on stage for a second encore, a less than ten minute Waves > Basis. Although it is perfunctory, it demonstrates just how important it was to the band that they tied up their loose ends.

Since Basis was a microcosm of the band’s state, it continued to grow in spring and fall 1999. The first Basis of the spring tour was played at the legendary Trocadero show on 4/9/99. The classical cover The Thieving Magpie was debuted out of the main jam, and the ending was once again played in a Waves > Basis combination, this one considerably more fleshed out and considered by some to be the greatest Biscuits jam of all time. Another contender for that same accolade can be found on 4/17/99 in the legendary Shimmy > Basis pairing, the second Basis of the tour. After a solid standalone version on 4/23/99, another legendary Basis was performed at the storied Wetlands Preserve on 5/1/99, with a Basis > Vassillios > Basis anchoring the first ever palindrome set. After three out of the first four Bases of tour being legendary versions, the song remained a consistent heavy hitter for the remainder of the tour, with a particularly solid standalone version performed on 5/27/99, and with an excellent split version sandwiching the second inverted Boop on 6/13/99. Another important development for the song occurred on 5/14/99. Jamming on the middle section had become more common in the winter, but was taken to a new level when Basis was jammed out of and split at the middle section, with a particularly intense and primally psychedelic jam from Bernstein back into the Basis bass slaps.

There weren’t many significant developments to Basis in fall 1999, although just about every version from this tour is worth hearing. The most worthwhile of these are 10/6/99 (a 40 minute version widely considered the greatest standalone) and 10/28/99 (in addition to one of the best endings ever, Basis is teased and faked out throughout the show and as part of the “Spagopera”). The final Basis of the year was ending only, used as the final destination for the 100+ minute Akira jam, one of the Biscuits’ crowning achievements.

With the departure of Marc Brownstein from the band at the beginning of 2000, Basis entered its first lull in years. The first show of the year, 3/11/00, featured a Basis with Sammy on bass and Mauricio on percussive synths (the format that all the original Munchkin Invasions and Crickets were played in). The same lineup played a Basis > Helicopters > Basis sandwich on 4/22/00. These versions have their merits but overall are particularly ineffective, especially in the composition. The song was played twice more before the core four properly reunited, in full on 6/27/00 with Jordan Crisman on bass, and ending only on 8/19/00 with Pauly Herron (of Electron et al.) on percussion. The 6/27 version is particularly worthwhile, with a triumphant and unconventional intro jam and a powerful ending.

On 10/13/00, the core four performed a full Basis for the first time since 10/28/99. The roughly 38 minute version featured drawn out intro and main jams and a perfunctory middle jam, and signalled the beginning of the second golden age of Basis. Although the 10/13 version has moments of staleness, particularly in the main jam, it is a very solid version overall, and just about every version from the rest of the year is worthwhile. In particular are 10/21/00, 10/27/00 and 11/11/00: 10/21/00 is split up and sandwiched between Jigsaw Earth, in a brilliant Jigsaw > Basis > Jigsaw > Basis > Jigsaw segment that is one of the best of the year, and standalone Bases open the second set of 10/27/00 and the first set of 11/11/00, and these are often regarded as the year’s strongest. A unique dyslexic Basis can be found on 11/3/00; the show opens with the tag section, and an otherwise full Basis is played in the second set, with a full Barfly replacing the tag.

The golden age of Basis continued into 2001, although there aren’t many important versions from the spring tour. Some major exceptions include 4/1/01 Basis > Waves (><) > Basis and the excellent 33 minute standalone on 4/6/01. Basis made an important comeback on 7/5/01, with a majestically interwoven pairing of Crickets and Basis anchoring the second set. In the fall tour Basis was a regular powerhouse once again. The second show of the tour, and final show at the Wetlands Preserve, 9/2/01, featured a powerful 35 minute standalone Basis in the third set. 9/15/01 Basis > Ape (><) > Basis is a fan favorite segment and considered by many to be among the best versions of both songs. And 11/1/01 features a spectacular Basis that cracks the 40 minute mark, the first to do so. But perhaps the strongest version of the year can be found on 9/12/01, in which the band delivered a powerful and emotionally resonant Basis the day after the national tragedy.

Spring 2002 suffered an even greater dearth of meaningful Bases than did spring 2001. The tour in general was extremely song-heavy and lighter on stretched out jams, so it isn’t altogether surprising that a powerhouse like Basis suffered. Those interested in the era should check out the 3/6/02 version (generally considered to precede the overly song-y stretch of spring 02) and maybe 4/29/02 (from a Meatcamp set that is overflowing with heavy hitters), but the rest of the tour can largely be written off. Basis began to get interesting again in the summer (worth checking out are 8/17/02 Judy’s > Basis and 8/24/02 Frog Legs > Basis) and by the fall it had once again attained heavy hitter status. The polarizing “almost palindrome” of 10/2/02 is bookended by an excellent Basis, and 10/26/02 features another strong version of the song, but the two titans of 02 are undoubtedly 10/18/02 (Rock Candy > King of the World > Aquatic Ape (><) > Basis is some of the best music of the year) and 11/9/02 (the entire thing is excellent, but the intro is transcendent). 11/9/02 was the last Basis of the year, making 2002 the only year in which Basis was not played over the New Year’s run.

Although in previous years Basis seemed to dip in quality during the spring tours, spring 2003 is actually a particularly strong era for Basis. The first Basis of the year was played on 4/6/03, a 46 minute standalone (the longest standalone at the time and for over a decade afterward) that is highly regarded as one of the best. The next version of the year, 4/17/03, is another highly regarded version, particularly for the intro and middle jams. The other versions from the tour (split versions on 4/25/03 and 5/4/03, and an ending only version on 5/26/03) are solid as well. In the summer, Basis was played on 7/2/03, and then sat on the shelf for a then-unprecedented 17 shows, until it was dusted off for a monster final-set-centerpiece at the mythical Trancemission festival on 8/16/03. It then sat on the shelf for a whopping 27 shows (still its longest gap ever) until it was played again on 12/31/03. This Basis was central to the New Year’s Eve gimmick: It closed out the first set, but was left unfinished as the band jammed with the New Deal into their setbreak set. At the end of the New Deal’s set, the Biscuits gradually came out for another New Deal/Biscuits jam that segued into the end of Basis, complete with New Year’s countdown.

In the twilight years of 1.0, Basis stayed in the rotation but seemed to have lost some of its luster. It was played six times total with Sammy in 2004-2005. Of these, the only one really worth hearing is the standalone version played 12/29/04 as the second part of the encore. Fans who left to beat the traffic as the band started up Eulogy were no doubt dismayed to learn that, not only had the band treated the remaining faithful to an excellent Basis, they had reprised the jam that would eventually become Gangster in the intro jam.

With Allen joining the band, Basis regained its status as a once-every-five-shows song (from 2003-2005 it was more a once-every-eight-or-nine-shows song). Allen’s first Basis was on New Year’s Eve 2005, and he tackled the song on sixteen occasions in 2006. As he grew more and more comfortable with his place in the band, so too did the Bases he played become gradually more confident. There aren’t many must-hear versions from 2006, but they can be found towards the end of the year: 9/23/06, 11/4/06, and especially 11/25/06 all have moments of greatness.

Like the song’s golden age in 1.0, the golden age for Basis in 2.0 coincides with the golden age of Biscuits 2.0, beginning sometime in 2007 and ending sometime in 2009. The first extant version of 2007, 5/20/07, was the first best Basis of the year, and strong versions from the summer and fall include 6/28/07, 8/17/07, 10/12/07 and 11/4/07. In early 2008 monster versions of Basis were incorporated into jam-heavy three and four song sets, such as 1/19/08’s I-Man > Nughuffer (><) > Basis or 3/1/08’s Triumph > Shelby (><) > Basis (both excellent versions). In the summer, strong versions of Basis were played at major festival appearances, including 6/7/08 at Starscape and 6/13/08 at Bonnaroo.

2009 was arguably the strongest year for Basis in 2.0, with 6/5/09 and 9/19/09 being some of the best versions of the song for any era. In 2009 the three-part Basis became ubiquitous. 1/24/09 saw Basis split into beginning/middle, end and tag, but the first proper three-part Basis since 1/30/97 was played on 2/27/09 (beginning) and 2/28/09 (middle and end). This is, in fact, the first four-part Basis (in practice, the most number of pieces Basis can be split into), since the tag is played separately as well. Another three-part Basis was played over the New Year’s run, and the trend continued into later years.

After 2009 there were considerably fewer meaningful versions of Basis, although the song remained a catalog staple and guaranteed crowd pleaser. 1/31/10 and 3/15/10 are solid pre-wristgate fare, although nothing groundbreaking, and 7/8/11 is a strong portion of a strong show. Basis was played almost exclusively as a three-part or four-part song in 2012 and 2013, and remained stagnant until an earth-shattering standalone performed at the Mann Center on 9/27/13 as part of City Bisco. Breaking the 47 minute mark, it is the longest standalone Basis played, breaking the record previously held by 4/6/03 by over a minute. In addition to its length, it is widely considered the strongest Basis of the setbreak era (and one of the strongest of any era).

Basis continued to recover ground as the band did, and was mostly solid in 2014 and 2015. In 2016, Basis entered what might be called a silver age, with mostly solid versions appearing over the next four years. Basis also became more common, played a whopping seven times each year in 2016 and 2017, the most since 2010. After a few strong performances in 2016, most notably 2/6/16 at the Fillmore Philadelphia, Basis was inverted for the first and only time on 7/16/16 at Camp Bisco in one of the most memorable sets of the setbreak era. 2017 is similarly solid, with strong versions on 2/4/17 at the Fillmore, and 12/31/17 at the Playstation Theater, in what was also the most recent three-part Basis.

After two strong years, Basis was not played for over six months and 18 shows (its second-longest show gap and longest since 2003). It made its reappearance as the encore of the final night of Camp Bisco, 7/14/18, and was played twice more that year. The latter, played 12/28/18, is a particularly unique and interesting version with a wide variety in synth choices. After another strong performance on 1/31/19, Basis disappeared for another 18 shows until reappearing in November, its longest calendar gap. The Basis delivered on 12/31/19 is excellent, one of the strongest versions of the past decade.

Basis has been a staple of the band’s catalog for decades, nearly since it was written. It has been played more times than any other song except for two: Morph and I-Man. Disappearances of more than ten shows are very infrequent.

history:
Larry Chasnoff, Marc, and a mutual friend of ours, Keith Koslov, all spent their summers growing up together in upstate NY at a place called Schroon Lake.

I went to high school with Keith and knew Marc as his annoying prep school friend, way too soft for us public school Brooklyn thugs. Then a bunch of us went to see Phish in Sugarbush in 95, and Marc started telling about this band he was in, and I started telling him about this idea I had for a book.

Walking around the lots a kid from Penn recognized Marc from his band and got all excited. I thought to myself, "hmmm, if the book thing doesn't work out, maybe I can ride Brownstein's coattails a little."

A few months later, as the Biscuits toiled in relative obscurity, we came out with the first Pharmer's Almanac. Only about 6 people worked on it, but we wanted to make it look more like a community project, so we put a lot of fake names in the staff box. It was a mix of names of people from Schoon Lake (Nick Weiss) and completely absurd names like Harvey Klopstein, Tariq Ali and Shep Williams.

When Marc and Keith saw the book a few months later, they thought the fake names were hysterical. While I wasn't there, I assume they spent the next few hours making fun of Chasnoff and I on every possible level. And at some point Keith pulled out a guitar. The rest was history.

So that's where the song came from. ("Klopstein and Cabot/ we just won't have it/we know exactly who you are/Tariq and Shep Williams/ pages we'll fill'em/ but phony names will only go so far.)

I was all excited that I had a song with my name in it until people started coming up to me and asking "Hey, why did you get sued by Phish?"

I want to state, for the record, that we never were sued by Phish, never threatened to be sued by Phish, and never had any legal issues with Phish regarding the Almanac. Every interaction we've had with management has been positive.

We caught a lot of grief in the early years from about a dozen people on rec.music.Phish (I know, what a shocker, someone getting grief on an Internet discussion group) but we never got the same from management.

I'm not actually sure where the "You're getting sued/bummer dude" line came from, but I think it had to do with the fake names or maybe some of the flack we were getting on the Internet.

The Almanac ended up selling about 70,000 copies, but at some point I got tired of going to Phish shows and decided it was a lot more fun to see the Disco Biscuits.

~Andy Bernstein

Although its lyrics were never cerebral, Bernstein & Chasnoff connects the band to greater jamband lore. Musically the song is not much more complicated: There are two verses, each followed by a chorus, a bridge and chorus, a jam section, and a triumphant ending. At various points in its history, the ending has contained a bonus section (referred to as “Smell The Funk” only after it had been shelved).

For its first year, B&C did not contain any jamming of note (refer to 1/30/97 for some truly bizarre sound effects in the pre-Trancefusion era). Trancefusion era versions of 97 (of which 11/17 and 11/18 are extant) do little to suggest the song’s eventual heavy hitter potential. Beginning early in 1998, the song became a vehicle for some of the band’s most interesting early experimentations. 2/26/98 is of particular note, a 25-minute version that contains elements of what would make the song great. Even more significant is 3/21/98, the “Techno B&C,” and what is considered to be the first “Perfume version” of any song. The song remained strong, if slightly less noteworthy, for the remainder of 1998. Already its M.O. was becoming pretty clearly established—the song would regularly depart from blissful type one territory for spacey, sinister territory, and was the earliest example of this style of exploratory jamming.

One of the first jams of 1999 was a B&C jam, in the early morning hours of January 1. This B&C > Nughuffer was likely the greatest example of pure Trancefusion yet played at the time. The song stayed strong through 1999 (a high water mark for both the band and the song), with standout versions played on 4/24, 4/30, 5/5, and 9/11 of that year. In particular, the latter two are frequently cited as the strongest versions of the song.

The band took a hiatus from B&C during its author’s departure from the band, but it returned with a vengeance at Camp Bisco, split-up dyslexically over 8/25/00 and 8/26/00. Despite the fewer shows played in 2000, there is no shortage of strong B&Cs from the fall tour. Of these 10/27 is thoroughly unique, and a sleeper choice for best ever, while 12/28/00 is more reminiscent of the classic 1999 style B&C.

After 2000, B&C faded a bit into the background, although some standout versions do exist from this era. 4/24/01 received some attention for its inclusion in Steele’s Picks, 9/6/01 contains some fantastic fall 2001 jamming and one of the early Sound 1s, and 10/5/02 is remarkably strong (of course, as is everything from that show). 11/29/03 is a lesser-known but very interesting version, which may be the first to be jammed out of the bridge rather than the main jam section.

B&C was played just thrice in 04 and once in 05 before Allen joined the band. After a few versions in the winter and spring shows, it was absent for nearly the whole of 06, from 4/26 until 12/29. The 12/29 version is a much-loved mashup with Joy to the World, and features the return of the Smell the Funk section, shelved in January 1999 and busted out only once on 5/5/01. It would be played on every 07 version and then shelved again indefinitely.

2007 would be B&C’s second golden era, as nearly every version from that year is excellent and highly regarded. After the fairly standard Jam Cruise version, it was split three ways for the first time at the legendary Starland Ballroom run on 2/17, which featured numerous debuts, Allen first-timers, and bustouts. While it didn’t surface over the spring tour, the standalone version that opened Camp Bisco VI is probably the strongest standalone with Allen. In the fall tour, 10/16 is a particularly strong version (flying slightly under the radar due to a lack of available soundboard) and 11/1 contains the first jam into the beginning of the song with Allen, and since 4/4/02.

B&C was only played twice in 08, although 4/19/08’s monster inverted version (first inversion with Allen and first since 7/23/03) is a must-hear. After a single performance each in the winter tour and spring tour of 09, B&C was played six times in the four months from 10/3/09 to 1/28/10. Each of those 6 versions is inverted. In the post-wristgate era, B&C rarely produces a memorable jam, with two glaring exceptions: the stellar and spacey 2/3/17 B&C > Voices > B&C, and the monster dyslexic beginning that opened the second set of 10/19/20.

history:
Inarguably one of the longest songs in the Biscuits catalog, 42 features repetitive trancey guitar riffs and catchy synth hooks, cryptic lyrics, and the potential for a powerful peak that, at times, would cause even the most seasoned vets to incorrectly call Run Like Hell. 42 alienated some fans at first with its lengthy verses and slow pre-choruses, and at its first performance, 4/3/03, the only jam was a short and very type one solo. The band did not waste any time fleshing out 42, however: it was segued into the first performance and split up by its fifth, 4/16/03--into Run Like Hell, unsurprisingly. By 4/26/03, which featured a standalone 42, the song had a reliable jam section. It was inverted for the first time on 7/26/03, a show which features numerous other setlist innovations such as the second inverted Aceetobee, the first three-part Buddha, and the first split unfinished Shimmy.

The band continued to flesh out 42 for the remainder of Sammy’s tenure, but it wasn’t until Allen joined the band that the song’s full potential as trance juggernaut was realized. It was played twice over New Year’s Run 2005, and nineteen times in 2006 (the most times played after 2003). The song quickly became a centerpiece of the band’s spacey psychedelic sound of 06-07. Important versions include 5/4/06 (mainly for the jam into it but a solid full version as well), 11/22/06, and 6/9/07.

If the song fared well in the early era of 2.0, it was perhaps at its peak in the high-energy later years of 2.0, late 08-early 10. Numerous high-energy, exploratory versions abound from this era, such as 12/27/08, 2/15/09, 4/18/09 (widely regarded as the best standalone version), and 6/6/09.

42 remained a staple of the band's catalog through the setbreak years, with a brief renaissance in 2017-2018. 6/1/17 is a powerful 2009-esque version, while 10/20/18 and 12/29/18 recall more experimental early versions.

history:
Awol’s Blues is a pretty standard early Biscuits blues tune. It is fairly unremarkable except for the fact that it was played so often, a whopping sixty times in 1997-1998. The band so loved this tune that it found its way onto Uncivilized Area, the final song on the album.

After a few performances in 1999, the last of which being 9/24/99, Awol’s Blues returned to the shelf, a relic of the bygone pre-Trance-Fusion days. It was busted out on three occasions. The first was 7/28/02, representing a gap of 225 shows (just one more than the current gap). It was performed a few more times and then sat on the shelf for 111 shows until a one-time performance on 9/3/04. After that it sat on the shelf for the rest of the Sammy days and well into the Allen era, when it was busted out for one final performance on 12/29/12 after 491 shows. The Biscuits have not performed the song since.

history:
I say goodbye and walk away

One of many debuts of the storied 2007 Starland Ballroom run, Air Song, like many other debuts from 2/15/07, sat on the shelf for several months after its first performance before entering the rotation. It was a little over a year later, in the same building where it was debuted, that Air Song was played for the second time.

Air Song was played 17 times, on average roughly every 3.5 shows, in 2008. Although the first few versions were played as a standalone, it quickly developed into a jam vehicle and setlist juggernaut in the early days of 08. Early standout versions include 3/23/08 and 4/2/08 (the first split-up version). On 4/12/08 Air Song was inverted for the first time, and on 4/25/08 it was used to bookend a palindrome set. The remaining Air Songs of the year were played unfinished or full.

After 2008, Air Song became a much rarer occurrence. It was played only five times in 2009 (once every 20 shows on average), but all five versions are excellent. 1/16/09 saw the return of the inverted Air Song, which features a spectacular and unconventional jam back into Spacebird. On 4/4/09 it was used as the meat in a solid Voices sandwich. 6/27/09 might be the best known Air Song simply because of how legendary the segment is: Story > Pilin’ > Air Song > Story. The jam out of Air Song is one of two absolute must-hear jams from that segment, but the jam into it merits attention as well. 9/22/09 featured a four song second set with fantastic jams into and out of Air Song, and 10/10/09 featured an excellent Air Song sandwiched within House Dog.

After 2009 the quality of the average Air Song began to dip, while it still remained a rarity. Although it was never “shelved” (besides the time between its first and second performances) it became increasingly rare after 2011, played only once per year in 2012 and 2013, twice in 2014, once in 2015 and twice in 2016. After this, it had a brief resurgence, played three times in 2017 four times in 2018 (or roughly once every 9.3 shows, the most frequently since 08) and three times in 2019.

history:
The median debut of the Hot Air Balloon (The Overture, Fiddler, Voices and Mulberry’s debuted before, while The Very Moon, Eulogy, Waves and Hot Air Balloon debuted after), Bazaar is very arguably the technical high-water mark of the entire opera. The composition consists of a slow intro riff evocative of Middle Eastern styles of music, a faster instrumental section, a verse chorus combo, a very slow breakdown and bridge verse, a second faster instrumental section, a second verse and chorus, the same fast instrumental section from the intro, a third verse, and a closing riff reprising a section from Above the Waves. Due to its rigid and relatively complex composition, it is rarely played and even more rarely jammed. Over its history, the “jam section” in Bazaar Escape has moved multiple times.

The debut of Bazaar Escape, like the other Hot Air Balloon songs, occurred at the tail end of 1998, on 11/14 at Carnegie Mellon. The debut version was considerably more adventurous than most versions; it is jammed into out of an unfinished Boop. For the next few months, an intro jam was the most improv fans could expect from Bazaar Escape. It was more frequently either played as a standalone, or, on special occasions such as performances of the full Hot Air Balloon opera, segued into Mulberry’s Dream by way of a composed bridge lifted from Voices Insane.

Although it continued to be played primarily as a standalone in 1999, there were significant developments to the song. On 1/28/99, for the first time, Bazaar Escape was outro’d. The jam emerges from the Waves instrumental section and slowly evolves into an Aceetobee intro. Less than a month later, Bazaar Escape was outro’d a second time, this time prior to the Waves section. Unlike the first outro, this jam maintains the high energy level of the ending of Bazaar Escape and evolves into a type two vehicle.

For most of its history, any jamming on Bazaar Escape took the form of an outro or (more typically) an intro jam. It was split up twice in 1999. The first, 5/11/99, was part of a very scripted Hot Air Balloon opera show, and all the segues around the song were jamless (the song was split seamlessly in the middle of a verse). The second split version was performed as part of the very different “Spagopera” of 10/28/99; the segue out of Bazaar is jamless, but the jam back into the ending is spectacular. Here, the split in the song takes place in the slow bridge, preceding the “Corrinado hides down an alley” verse.

After a whopping 37 performances in 1999, Bazaar Escape became a rarity. Its first performance in 2000 was 6/27/00 with Jordan Crisman on bass. After this performance, it was played five times in the fall tour and once more over the New Year’s run. The most significant of these was 11/24/00 at the Trocadero, which was a jammed out extravaganza: it has a solid intro jam out of Shimmy and is split up, this time out of the fast instrumental section before the final verse. This would be the jam section in Bazaar for almost all future versions. Although the standard was always a jamelss standalone, Bazaar was jammed out on a few other memorable occasions in the latter half of Sammy’s tenure, including 4/4/01 (one of only two three-part versions) and 7/26/02 (the midpoint of the famous “almost palindrome” set).

Bazaar became increasingly rare in the final years of 1.0, played only 7 times from 03-05. Allen took his first stab at the song at Camp Bisco V, 8/25/06, segued out of the first inverted Spaga. This bold setlisting signaled that a more adventurous approach to Bazaar was to come, and almost none of the versions from 06-08 were true standalones. It was used as the landing pad to a massive Dribble outro on 11/2/06, as the meat of a palindrome (and out of a Moshi-Fameus jam no less) on 11/10/06, and, perhaps most memorably, as the three-part centerpiece to the massive second set from 12/31/06, complete with New Year’s countdown.

The golden age of Bazaar Escape continued into 07. Its first appearance was 5/17/07, which featured a gorgeous ambient outro jam into Robots. Other significant appearances over the summer include 7/8/07, in which it was used to sandwich the opening segment, and 7/19/07, the first and so-far-only inverted version. Almost every version from the fall tour was jammed out and split up, usually across multiple dates.

The first Bazaar of 08 is considered by many to be the definitive version. It is segued into from Rockafella, has a gorgeous psychedelic space jam in the usually very staid breakdown, and a fantastic main jam. Unlike many others from the era, it is not split. Bazaar was played ending-only two more times in 08 (and ever), 4/12/08 and 6/9/08, and a jamless standalone on 12/11/08 signaled the end of the golden age of Bazaar.

After 08, the jamless standalone Bazaar once again became the norm, and the song became once again a perennial rarity. It was last jammed out of on 4/26/13, last jammed into on 4/22/16, and has been relegated to a once-every-couple-of-years bustout.

title: Abraxas
history:
Dragons Don’t Eat Onions

Supposedly named for the famous coffee and cannabis shop in Amsterdam (and not the Santana album) that the band visited during Jam in the Dam 06, Abraxas was debuted as part of the three day Wind at Four to Fly release party at Higher Ground in April 2006. Abraxas features intricate riffs and chilling atmospheric synths, possibly the most musically complex and challenging of the instrumentals that debuted in the early 2.0 period.

The song was consistently played as a jamless standalone through the spring of 06, with little to no variation in versions. The earliest version of note was played 6/24/06, during the Biscuits’ first visit to Starscape; it was segued into out of the composition of Rock Candy in a “DJ” style segue, played in full, and outro’d into the end of Rock Candy. The second night of Camp Bisco V, 8/26/06, featured the first properly jammed out Abraxas.

Abraxas became more of a jam vehicle in the fall of 2006. 11/1/06 features the first inversion of Abraxas, and the overwhelming majority of future versions would be played in this format (only one of the six Abraxases played in fall 2006 was not inverted). Abraxas was played standalone a couple of times in early 07, somewhat regressively, but by the summer and especially fall it had become a full-fledged powerhouse. The unfinished Abraxas opener from the Tractorbeam show 6/26/07 at the Chameleon Club stands as a spectacular achievement in patient, atmospheric jamming. The fall tour produced such spectacular versions as 10/23/07 and 11/3/07, both considered some of the best ever.

Abraxas remained strong throughout the 2.0 era. 1/17/08 and 7/18/08 stand out as particularly strong 08 versions. Somewhat overlooked is 4/3/08, which is also noteworthy as the only split-up Abraxas. The song flourished in 09 especially, with 1/18/09, 1/31/09, 4/20/09, 6/6/09, and 12/26/09 all highly regarded versions. Also of note is 11/20/09, the last Abraxas ever played as a standalone. Abraxas was less consistent in 2010, but this history would be incomplete without a mention of 7/16/10, a fantastic version whose notoriety is in part based on the introduction of lasers to the Biscuits’ light rig.

In 2009 Phantasy Tour users wrote lyrics for the song. To date, the band has not performed these lyrics.

Abraxas has remained a staple of the band’s catalog since its debut and beyond the setbreak era. Because of the complicated main riffs, the song is something of a bellwether for the overall state of the band (and especially Barber). history:
After the tepid response to Planet Anthem, the band continued to push out new material in summer and fall 2010 that would form the heart of their next album, Otherwise Law Abiding Citizens. The first of these songs to debut was Bombs, which soon established its role as a heavy hitter within the catalog. It was played within a massive medley for its debut at Camp IX, and for its sophomore performance at Dewey Beach (widely considered the greatest version). It has never been played standalone, is rarely followed by a comma in setlists (the last time was 3/27/11), and has only once been preceded by one (1/28/12).

Bombs saw a resurgence during 2014, in which two versions (8/1 and 12/26) produced sprawling type two jams. 3/26/16 at the Capitol Theater is another much-loved recent version. Bombs has seen steady play since its debut, appearing at least once every year except for 2020. It is the only 2010 OLAC debut to not be shelved for more than a year.

history:
Beyond a paleocentric world with all our people shaped in threes, The only way I get around is with some mild insanity.

The first debut of 1998, Mindless Dribble signalled an important shift in the band’s style and songwriting maturity. It’s challenging lyrics and aggressive style placed it in contrast to the faux-hippie neo-psychedelia of 97-95.

The first few performances of Dribble were completely free of improv, but within a little more than a month the band was beginning to carve out the song’s nascent jam section. There is a tremendous observable growth throughout the year, with at least one must-hear version, 12/30/98 (also noteworthy as the first "happy" Dribble). Other noteworthy early versions include 4/18/98 and 5/2/98.

The song became a major jam vehicle in 1999, the year where most of the strongest versions can be found. The jam section remained fairly standard throughout the year, with a few notable deviations, e.g. the demented, primal 10/28/99 and the fairly blissful 12/30/99 (another "happy" Dribble). The song remained strong through 2000, with noteworthy versions including 10/31/00 (the longest version to date) and 10/6/00, in which the chord progression that eventually gave rise to The Big Happy, Highwire, and I Remember When was debuted.

Dribble remained a strong selection in 2001, with the split-up "happy" Dribble from 3/31/01 widely regarded as one of the best. The song also underwent some important developments in this year. On 4/20/01 (fittingly) the “dub” version of Mindless Dribble was debuted, a part of the larger trend of dubbed versions of Biscuits songs that swept up both I-Man and Floodlights during April 2001. Later in the year, the song became the vehicle for the composed jam that would eventually become known as Strobelights and Martinis. Beginning on 9/1/01, and continuing through the month, every Dribble (with the exception of 9/21/01) would bear the hallmarks of this jam. The section was briefly reprised again in April 2003 and occasionally after Strobelights was debuted as its own song.

Although Dribble remained a staple of the catalog, its appearance grew less frequent in 2.0. It was never shelved, and was often split up to keep it interesting. When not split up, Dribble often fell into predictable patterns that made it less interesting than it had been in the 1.0 era (though exceptions to this rule exist--most notably the Red Rocks Dribble of 5/29/10).

Dribble continued to be a common presence throughout the setbreak era, being played, on average, around once every five or six shows (the striking exception to this is in 2018, when, excluding the dub version from Camp Bisco, Dribble was only played once the entire year). The song had a major renaissance during the "Setbreak is Over" tour of fall 2019. 11/16/19 and 11/17/19 each feature half of a strong split version, and arguably the strongest full version played with Allen took place on 12/13/19.

lyrics:
The waves make mountains, I've sailed with ease,
As wind gathers firmly in my canopy.
We dive through the mist to the autumn sun,
My vessel and its crew of twenty one, and we fly.

Through burgundy smoke and a fear of home,
Alas, my final mission to the great unknown.
As my thoughts betray me in flashes so bold,
I'm reminded of home where the coast shines like gold.

darkness, thunderstorm, a ship going down,
the crashing of rain and its deafening sound.
as the crew ties the sails blown aside by the wind,
crashing from the waves come tumbling in and we fly.

Rolling like a cobra, one life to spend,
drifting through the heavens where the oceans they end.
and there's no longer the sea no longer the sun,
my ship and the waves have all swirled into one.

And i'm off past the vision, the line of the light,
Where oceans turn waterfalls, daytime turns night.
And no people return, no stories to tell,
And i watched through the door for the toll of the bell.

And we fly...

One with the raging wind,
Alive on the highest tides,
My ship at sail can climb a mountain,
Ride it to the sky.

Whoa...oh, he'll navigate!

Earlier up this morning, as I sit upon the bow,
In the distance, my homeland, but I just don't know how.
Years along the sea, and I thought I'd find the sun.
Once around the world, and now I think I'm done.

history:
Astronaut was debuted at the unannounced Boom Boom Room show on 8/8/01, along with Coat. Instrumentally, this version does not differ much from modern versions, but the lyrics bear little resemblance to the finished song. The basic structure of the first half of the song is the same as modern versions, two intro riffs, verse-chorus-verse-chorus, a peak, and a bridge consisting of a simple descending/ascending riff. In the first version, the bridge (commonly known as the Suspended in the Air, or SITA, section) is followed by a third verse. The chorus is not repeated, and the song ends rather abruptly without a jam.

The second version of Astronaut is nearly three times as long as the first. It was played at the band’s final show at the Wetlands Preserve, on 9/2/01. It is a considerably tighter version, and the new lyrics are much closer to finalized (they would remain largely unchanged throughout the rest of the year). After the SITA section, the band plays the peak section again (although Barber doesn’t play the peak in this version, he does in others), then an extended jam that returns to the peak. The band attempts to return to a final chorus after the second peak, but there is considerable confusion and this second version is aborted.

Astronaut was arguably played a third time on 9/9/01, although this is almost never counted. As Spacebirdmatingcall ends, a definite SITA jam is used to segue into House Dog Party Favor. Although this isn’t counted as a performance of Astronaut, it is fairly significant as the first jamming on the SITA section. Astronaut was played another ten times in 2001. Of these, seven had outro jams, with the band dropping back into a SITA-esque jam immediately following the closing chords.

After its performance over the 2001 New Year’s run, Astronaut was not played again until 4/4/02, as the first part of the encore. Here the lyrics are roughly 99% identical to modern versions, and the main jam develops more organically out of the SITA section (the “peak section” that the band would play after SITA is dropped). This is arguably the first split Astronaut, but the Peter Gunn in the Astronaut jam is sometimes notated as a tease. The first split Astronaut otherwise was begun on 8/9/02 and was finished on 8/11/02, and the first (and for years only) inverted Astronaut was 10/23/02. The 2001 style Astronaut outro was played a couple times in Spring 02, but after 5/1/02 it was retired.

Throughout the Sammy years, Astronaut remained a fairly regular staple in the catalog. Its most common year was 2002 when it appeared on average once every five shows. Astronaut was known for mellow housey jams, although the Sammy years produced some monster versions. 10/5/02 is usually considered the best of this, and perhaps of any, era. 9/19/01 is a significantly exploratory early version, and 4/18/03 is excellent as well, spawning a passage of gorgeous blissco that evolves to a triumphant inverted Confrontation. 5/31/03 saw the return of the outro jam, though played differently (without the SITA section) than it was in 01-02, and 7/25/03 is a unique version that is split up between the first and second verse.

After 2003, Astronaut became less common, and was only played six more times with Sammy in 2004-2005. 10/1/04, though nothing special musically, is significant as the first to be split up in the SITA section. 3/25/05 features the first substitution of “Yo Girl You Crazy” for “Take Me Too” in the chorus, but 8/26/05 is probably the best from this era, especially for the excellent outro jam into Stone (significant as both the first modern Astronaut outro and the only real jam into Stone).

When Allen joined the band, Astronaut was given a fresh start, and was played considerably more frequently: from 2006-2009, Astronaut was played on average once every 5-6 shows, or about as frequently as it was played in 2002. The spacey electronic style of 06-07 Biscuits proved fertile ground for the development of the SITA section as a jam vehicle, and pretty soon Astronaut was a two jam song.

Astronaut was one of the stronger songs in Allen’s early repertoire, with standout versions as early as 4/27/06 and 5/28/06. The fall of 2006 was a particularly strong tour for Astronaut. Important versions include 11/4/06 (featuring a powerful main jam and an even stronger outro jam into a Moshi Fameus drum section), 12/7/06 (the second inverted version, and first in over four years) and, most importantly, 11/19/06.

Astronaut reached its zenith in the peak years of 2.0, 2007-2009. After consistently strong versions in the early part of the year, particularly 7/8/07 (a 22 minute standalone if you include the hypnotic intro jam), the band took Astronaut to a new level on 10/9/07, with a spectacular 30+ minute version. Widely considered one of the best ever, the 10/9/07 Astronaut elevated the song to a new level, and landmark versions were performed on 11/1/07 (another best ever contender), 10/26/07 (spicy full version with a powerful main jam) and 10/19/07 (the third inverted version).

2008 was a little more hit-or-miss for Astronaut, but still produced some more than solid versions. 3/19/08 features the first ever three part Astronaut, evidence of the tremendous development of the SITA section as a jam vehicle during the Allen years. Easily the most significant Astronaut of 2008 is the monstrous 30+ minute standalone that opened the day set of Camp Bisco VII on 7/19/08. Universally acclaimed, this Astronaut features two extended and thematic jams, and is considered by many to be the finest Astronaut ever played. A strong dyslexic version at Holidaze, on 12/12/08 and 12/14/08, and its use as the countdown on 12/31/08, cemented 2008 as an important year for Astronaut.

Along with fall tour 2007, the other contender for the strongest era for Astronaut is 2009. Astronaut was solid for the whole year, but was especially strong in the spring and summer. In this era the SITA jam took on a life as its own; previously relegated to mellow and spacey type one status, the SITA jam was by the middle of the year capable of producing type two ragers. The SITA jam section became so strong that Astronauts split in the SITA section became more common than Astronauts split the traditional way: beginning with 4/20/09, of the eight split Astronauts of the year, five are split at the SITA jam. The whole year produced significant Astronauts, such as 2/14/09, 2/28/09, 9/17/09, 9/26/09 and 10/8/09; however, it is the Astronauts from spring and summer, such as 4/3/09 (notable mainly for the SITA jam), 4/20/09, 6/4/09 and 6/27/09, that are worth checking out.

After a few immensely strong years, the star of Astronaut began to fade in 2010 and 2011, when it became more of a rarity (played on average once every 7 shows in 2010 and once every 10-11 shows in 2011). Although it was never shelved, Astronaut’s longest gaps from the rotation occurred in this era, when it wasn’t played for twenty shows between 6/5/10 to 9/8/10 and 12/27/10 to 7/2/11. September 2010 featured a particularly interesting version in which the beginning and end were played on 9/8/10 and were “completed” by a performance of the SITA section on 9/11/10. The version from Camp Bisco X on 7/8/11, which bookends a large palindrome set, is worth checking out as well.

Astronaut became more of a frequent setlist staple in the destination era. In 2017, Astronaut was played a whopping seven times, or on average once every 4-5 shows (making 2017 the year Astronaut was played most frequently), but in 2018 Astronaut was played only three times, or on average once every 12-13 shows (making 2018 the year Astronaut was played the least frequently). The 2017 versions, particularly 2/3/17 and 5/26/17, are standouts from the setbreak era, and 11/2/18, while notably sloppy, features a great theme that builds to the ending. 2019 features a few unique uses of Astronaut, including 1/25/19 and 7/20/19 where parts of Astronaut were "mashed up" with other songs, and one version, 12/27/19, that is considered among the best versions of the decade.

title: Boom Shanker
history:
The penultimate Conspirator cover by debut date and the distant second place in play count, Boom Shanker is arguably the strangest of the four. While Orch Theme, Commercial Amen, and Liquid Handcuffs all provide crowd-pleasing, high energy electronica, Boom Shanker is typically a mellow dub vehicle. Because of its vastly different sound, it was polarizing to many fans at the time of its debut at the second night of Camp Bisco V, with many hating it and many others cheering for the new era of Biscuits sound that it portended.

Boom Shanker was far from a staple during the fall tour, when it was played on average about once every five shows. Most of these versions are solid and showcase a large jam potential. The first has an extended, dreamy dub jam and a spacey outro. Most of the fall versions have at least a segue in or out. Of the 06 versions, best known is probably 9/23/06, which segues into a full-blown Basis intro.

2007 saw the song come into its own decisively. 2/17/07 opens with a particularly notable version, the first to break the type one mold. Here, the usual dub vehicle quickly departs for an infectious untz theme. Besides fall 06, Boom Shanker saw most consistent play in spring/summer 07, when it was played about once every seven shows. Of these, 6/9/07 (part of a massive set two medley at Starscape) and 8/16/07 (first night of Camp Bisco VI) are probably best known, but 7/10/07, featuring a fast paced minimalist jam into the rare Save the Robots intro, should be on any listener’s radar. Despite only being played once over the legendary fall tour of 2007 (in probably the most forgettable show), Boom Shanker closed out the year strong, with two highly regarded performances in December: 12/14/07 at the first Holidaze, and 12/28/07 during the New Year’s Run.

From 2008-2010, the band eased up on Boom Shanker and it became even more of a rarity. The three extant versions from 2008 are mostly unremarkable, but the song came back in a big way on 9/24/09 after a gap of 76 shows. The famous “Shimmy Shanker” sandwich is universally acclaimed as the greatest Boom Shanker ever played, and one of the greatest Biscuits segments of all time. The song made a few more appearances in 2009 and early 2010, and then, around the same time as two of the other three Conspirator originals, was retired.

Possibly due to Conspirator backlash, or possibly for some other reason, Boom Shanker stayed on the shelf for almost eight years, until it was finally busted out on 4/20/18 after 262 shows. It was played a few more times from then to the present, probably most notably on 7/19/19 when the band played a second “Shimmy Shanker” sandwich. It remains a perennial rarity, appearing every 1-2 years since its 2018 bustout.

history:
Arguably the silliest song in the Biscuits’ catalog, Aquatic Ape is also one of the oldest: its debut is preceded only by the debuts of Nughuffer and Down to the Bottom. Its silly lyrics and composition are contrasted by a generally dark jam section bookended by an infectious and simple guitar riff.

Despite having been around longer than most songs, Aquatic Ape has always been something of a rarity, having been played less than a hundred times total. Aquatic Ape was played less than ten times in every year but 1999.

1999 was arguably the strongest and most important year for Ape. Traditionally, Aquatic Ape is played with a relaxed dub-style jam, and it was played this way through the middle of 1999. 6/11/99 is notable as the first Aquatic Ape not to be played with a dub style jam (also the first, and one of the only, to not feature the riff that serves as the segue to the song’s jam and peak), and it was played instead in a simple trance style. In the fall of 1999, Ape was played three times. The first, 9/11/99, was unfinished, and was the first jungle style Ape. The other two, on 10/6/99, and 10/10/99, were both ending only, and while the 9/11 version was incomplete, it would be a stretch to say either of these versions were intended to complete it. This was a very progressive setlisting move for the time, when songs were usually played in full or completed.

After 10/10/99, Aquatic Ape sat on the shelf for 35 shows (for about half of these, its author, Marc Brownstein, was out of the band) until it was reintroduced at Camp Bisco II on 8/25/00. Here Aquatic Ape was inverted for the first time (only the fourth song to ever be inverted) as part of a second set palindrome. This Ape, as well as the others from this year, are all played jungle style. The jungle style Ape was prevalent for the rest of its history, but the dub style Ape made occasional appearances, notably on 12/31/01 at the request of Max Dawson, and on 10/18/02, an inverted version widely considered the greatest Aquatic Ape ever.

When Allen joined the band, Aquatic Ape made a brief resurgence before becoming even more of a rarity. On 2/04/06, Allen played Ape for the first time, segueing into Mr. Don for the show’s encore. This was the first Aquatic Ape in over a year, a gap of 26 shows. Ape was played three more times in 2006, with all but the final, on 12/28/06 at the Sonar, played in the jungle style.

After 2006, Ape sat on the shelf for over two years for its longest hiatus, a gap of 174 shows, until it was performed at the Electric Factory on 4/17/09. The storied three set show also featured the bust-outs of Eulogy (99 shows) and Wet (129 shows). After this perfunctory performance, Ape sat on the shelf for another year and a half before it was played again on 9/1/10 (a gap of 118 shows).

After 2010, Ape was upgraded from perennial rarity to once-or-twice a year status. It was played at least once every year in this time period, with the exception of 2015. The vast majority of these have been inverted, with more than two inverted versions for every other iteration since 2010. Since 2016, Aquatic Ape has only been played inverted. As Aquatic Ape has become something more of a staple, so too has the dub version. It has only been played with the dub jam five times since 12/28/06, but all of those versions were played after 2010: 1/23/11, 5/31/17, 4/19/18, 12/9/18, 5/23/19, were all played with dub jams.

history:
A sure-to-please rowdy blues song about drinkin’, Barfly was a staple of the band’s frat party days and earliest tours. It made its way into the stylistic hodgepodge that was the band’s first studio album, Encephalous Crime, where it is the final studio track. Barfly follows a very predictable format from which it rarely deviates: verse, chorus, verse, chorus, keyboard solo, bridge, guitar solo, verse, chorus.

Barfly was played 40 times in 1998, more than any other year. It was in 1998 that Barfly was jammed out for the first (and only) time. On 6/4/98 an unfinished Barfly segued into a drum solo ended the show, and 6/5/98 opened with a long intro jam into Barfly (supposedly intended to complete the night prior, although it, too, is unfinished) jammed into the ending of Run Like Hell. Besides being the only jammed out Barfly, it also marked the first time the Biscuits finished a song from an earlier show.

Barfly became steadily more rare beginning in 1999. After appearing semi-regularly in the winter and spring tours, it was played only twice in the fall before being shelved for nearly a year between October 1999 and 2000 for a gap of 32 shows (what was then a significant absence). It was played four times in 2000 and then eight each in 2001 and 2002 (although this represented a decline in frequency). From 2003 to the end of Sammy’s tenure in 2005, Barfly was even more scarce.

Allen’s arrival brought with it a brief resurrection of Barfly, which was played four times in three months in the earlier part of the year. However, it was only played once in the fall, after which it went from rarity to holographic status. It was played only once in 2007, after a gap of 75 shows, after which it sat on the shelf for two and a half years or 197 shows (its longest absence) when it was played at the Bisco Power Mission on 3/21/10 with Sammy on guitar.

It was played only a handful of times in the setbreak era: twice in 2013, once in 2014, once in 2018 and once in 2019. It’s performance on 4/27/19 is perhaps the most interesting part of a sub-par show; it provides the landing pad to the second set segment, making it the first Barfly to be jammed into (in fact, played in any way besides standalone) since 4/3/02.
